title: Reach 24 With Four Cards
statement:
You are dealt four cards in cards, each showing a number from 1 to 9. Using every card exactly once, in any order, combine them with +, −, × and ÷ and any parentheses you like. Return true if some expression equals exactly 24.

  • Division is real division: 8 ÷ 3 is 2.666…, not 2. Intermediate results may be fractions.
  • Every operator joins two values. A minus sign cannot be used on its own to negate a value.
  • Cards cannot be glued into multi-digit numbers: 1 and 2 cannot become 12.

examples.why: 6 ÷ (1 − 3 ÷ 4) = 6 ÷ 0.25 = 24. The only ways pass through fractions, so integer division would miss them.
No order, operators or grouping of four 7s gives 24.

hints: However the parentheses go, some operator is applied first, to two of the current values. What is left after that step?
Pick any two values, replace them by one of their results (a + b, a − b, b − a, a × b, a ÷ b, b ÷ a), and you have the same problem with one fewer value. Stop when one value is left.
Use floating point and accept a result within 1e-6 of 24, and never divide by (nearly) zero. Four values is a tiny search, so no pruning is needed.

explain.intuition:
Parentheses look like the hard part, but they only decide the order in which pairs get combined. Any expression is built by repeatedly taking two values and replacing them by one. So the search is: from a list of values, choose a pair, choose an operation, replace the pair by the result, recurse. With one value left, check whether it is 24.

The list goes 4 → 3 → 2 → 1, so there are at most 12 · 6 · 6 · 6 · 2 · 6 ≈ 9 000 leaves. Every bracketing and every order is covered, because the recursion tries every pair at every level. Fractions such as 3 ÷ 4 are real values here, so compare with a small tolerance instead of ===.
steps: If one value is left, return whether it is within 1e-6 of 24.
For every pair of positions i < j, build the list of the other values.
For each result of a + b, a − b, b − a, a × b, and a ÷ b / b ÷ a when the divisor is not zero, append it to the rest and recurse.
If any branch returns true, return true. Otherwise return false.
pitfalls: Using integer division, which drops the answers that go through fractions like [1, 3, 4, 6].
Trying only left-to-right evaluation, such as ((a op b) op c) op d. It misses (a op b) op (c op d), the shape needed for [1, 9, 1, 2].
Comparing floats with === 24. 8 ÷ (3 − 8 ÷ 3) is 23.999999999999996 in floating point.

complexity.time: O(1): a fixed search of a few thousand leaves

solutions.title: Every order, every operator, every bracket shape
solutions.idea: Try all 24 orderings of the cards, all 4³ operator choices and all 5 ways to bracket four operands, and evaluate each expression.

solutions.title: Combine two values, recurse on the shorter list
solutions.idea: Any expression is a sequence of pair merges. Pick two values, replace them by one result, and recurse until one value remains.

followups: Return one expression string that makes 24, not just true or false.
Generalise to n cards and any target. How fast does the search grow, and how would you memoise it?
